I think software engineering is becoming mentally exhausting in a very different way now.

Earlier the struggle was:
“How do I learn all this?”

Now the struggle is:
“What should I even focus on anymore?”

Every week there’s:

a new AI tool
a new framework
a new coding agent
a new workflow
a new prediction about developers becoming obsolete

And I think many students are silently overwhelmed.

They are not lazy,
it's because the industry feels totally unstable.

I’ve spoken to students who genuinely feel guilty for taking even a small break now.

They think:
“If I stop learning for 2 weeks, I’ll fall behind forever.”

That’s a horrible feeling to live with constantly.

The strange part is:
the more tools we get to improve productivity…
the more anxious people seem to become.

I think one of the most valuable skills in the next few years will simply be:
0. the ability to stay calm.
1. To ignore noise.
2. To focus deeply.
3. To build patiently.

Because the people who survive long-term in tech are usually not the fastest learners.

They are the most consistent thinkers.

That's why I always ask my students in my courses to "be curious" about everyting!

【Qwen 3.5 9B × Map-Reduce】小型LLMで業務の99%を自動化する最強の設計思想！

「ローカルLLMは実用性に欠ける」という常識を覆すシステム設計の秘訣を解説します！🚀

1️⃣ Map-Reduceパターンの採用
大きなタスクを小さなチャンクに分割して並列処理（Map）し、最後に統合（Reduce）する手法です。これにより、小型モデルの弱点であるコンテキスト窓の狭さをシステム構成で完璧にカバーします。

3️⃣ Pythonによるガードレール
LLMに丸投げせず、Pythonコードで処理の流れを制御。チェックポイントやリカバリ機能を実装し、業務レベルの安定性を実現しています。

title: Agents need real accountability, not another layer of surveillance. The moment an AI agent starts reading your files, routing decisions, remembering context, and acting on your behalf, its work has to
content:
Agents need real accountability, not another layer of surveillance. The moment an AI agent starts reading your files, routing decisions, remembering context, and acting on your behalf, its work has to be verifiable. Otherwise you’re left holding the bag when it quietly screws something up.

The usual fixes miss the mark completely. Either there’s zero audit trail and you have no idea what happened, or every token gets logged and suddenly your private workflow is one subpoena away from exposure. Both options are broken.

What @TheARCTERMINAL ARC is doing with ZKURT receipts actually solves the tension. It produces a compact, tamper-proof record that proves the agent performed specific reads, routes, memories, and actions without revealing the underlying data or reasoning. You can check the work later if you need to, but nobody else gets to peek inside.

That’s not flashy. It’s just the bare minimum we should demand before we let agents anywhere near important decisions. Without it we’re not building tools. We’re building black boxes we’ll eventually regret.

content:
New Stanford paper argues that, under equal reasoning budgets, one LLM usually solves multi-hop problems better than many coordinated ones.

The core point is almost embarrassingly simple.

A single agent keeps the whole problem in one internal chain of thought, while a multi-agent system has to slice that chain into messages, summaries, and handoffs.

Every handoff is a compression step.

And once reasoning is compressed, some information is easier to drop than to recover, which is why the paper leans on the Data Processing Inequality as a formal explanation rather than just an empirical hunch.

The experiments back that up across Qwen, DeepSeek, and Gemini on FRAMES and MuSiQue: when thinking-token budgets are matched, single-agent systems usually match or beat sequential, debate, role-based, and ensemble setups.

Here’s the part most people miss.

Many celebrated multi-agent gains may not be architectural gains at all. They often come from spending more test-time compute, surfacing more visible reasoning, or benefiting from evaluation quirks that make the pipeline look smarter than it is.

The paper is especially sharp when it looks for the boundary case instead of pretending the rule is universal.

When the single agent’s effective context is degraded by masking, substitution, or misleading distractors, multi-agent pipelines become more competitive and sometimes win, not because message passing is magical, but because structure can partially stabilize corrupted reasoning.

That is a much narrower and more useful claim than “more agents is better.”

It suggests the real trade-off is not single versus multi so much as latent reasoning versus external coordination, with context quality and compute accounting deciding which side looks stronger.

For multi-hop reasoning, the default should now be clear: start with one strong model, and treat extra agents as a repair strategy, not an upgrade.

----

Paper Link – arxiv. org/abs/2604.02460

Paper Title: "Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets"

title: A Chinese developer created an agent system in Claude Code to sell landing pages to small businesses and, working completely solo, serves about 47 clients a month, charging around $400 for each one.
content:
A Chinese developer created an agent system in Claude Code to sell landing pages to small businesses and, working completely solo, serves about 47 clients a month, charging around $400 for each one.

He built 7 agents on Claude Sonnet 4.6 capable of analyzing Google Maps in small cities, detecting businesses without websites or with totally outdated pages, and taking each opportunity all the way to a finished mockup, a promotional video, and a ready-to-send prospecting message.

No assistants.
No sales team.
No SDRs.

Just him, a MacBook, an iPhone, and an API key.

While traditional agencies maintain full teams to handle the same workflow, his only real costs are tokens and subscriptions to Lovable, Higgsfield, and Calendly.

The 7 agents operate coordinated by an orchestrator in Claude Code Router. The system consumes about 3 million tokens daily, and the average API spend is just around $480 a month.

They all work via MCP servers and share state using the file system, avoiding concurrency and shared memory issues. Even one of the agents lives directly on his iPhone and responds to leads while he's on the subway, in a taxi, or walking.

This was the main prompt he set up:

“You are the orchestrator of a solo agency that sells ready-made websites to local businesses…”

The key is that the system perfectly understands what it is, what its limits are, and what goals it must achieve.

It knows it must find leads automatically.
It knows it must convert each opportunity into a landing page, a video, and a sales message without human intervention.
And it knows exactly when to involve the owner.

The system runs 24/7:

Scout analyzes about 220 businesses daily and queues up 30 new leads.

Diagnoser generates diagnostics and personalized messages for each lead.

Builder creates between 3 and 5 complete landing pages for the best prospects.

Filmer produces a 10-second vertical video for each proposal.

Pitcher sends about 30 messages daily across 4 different channels with a response rate close to 14%.

Checker automatically reviews all messages before sending them.

Only when a deal exceeds $3,000 or the response rate drops below 12% does the system wake the owner.

And if he's on the subway or in a taxi at that moment, the Mobile agent automatically responds to the interested lead, schedules a call in Calendly, and returns the lead to the queue. The owner just has to hit “approve” and jump into the meeting.

Some real system logs:

“218 businesses analyzed in Austin, Denver, and Miami. 34 without websites, 19 with 2014-era sites, and 6 with reviews requesting redesigns.”

“30 messages sent. 14 responses. 5 positive. 3 Zooms scheduled.”

“Landing page created for a dental clinic. Responsive. 5 sections. Video rendering.”

“$3,400 deal exceeds approved limit. Sending for manual review.”

And the craziest part is that he has no dedicated servers or backend.

Just a local sandbox, an MCP router, a Claude API key, and that same key connected to his iPhone.

Of everything I've seen this year, this is probably the cleanest and most efficient example of a fully automated one-person agency:

$480 a month on APIs.
$18,800 in revenue.
7 prompts.
A file system.
And a phone in his pocket.

Save this before it's too late.

how much does it cost to run a Hermes Agent company

> Hermes: free, open source
> ChatGPT Pro: $200/month
> Claude Max: $200/month (or a similar amount in API)
> Telegram or Slack bot: free
> VPS to run 24/7: $6 to $9/month via Hetzner

total: $409/month

this setup gets you pretty far. you can achieve a lot by pairing two max plans together and distributing them across all your agent instances.

for example this is enough to run agent ops & marketing department for most boring businesses.

you will still need to optimize token usage and route the right model to the right job.

if I have a simple task like moving data from one place to another, I skip on the frontier models and use cheaper ones within the subscription. you can handle this with hermes tool routing on the backend, or by creating specific agent profiles per task type.

Q&A

> why would you need subscriptions for both ChatGPT and Claude?

because each model has different strengths. Claude is better at copywriting and strategic thinking, GPT works better at coding and structured outputs. you can ofc run with just one if you're okay with compromises.

a simple rule I follow (not rigid): if it's creative, Claude. if it's structured, GPT

> why choose subscriptions over API via OpenRouter?

I'm using models via API as well, but haven't found anything that matches the token usage of the max plans yet. This might change when the boosted token credits via OpenAI stops at the end of May.

content:
40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by end of 2027, per Gartner.

That number isn't an AI problem. It's an infrastructure problem.

Two kinds of "AI agent" projects exist right now.

Level 1: developer plus an AI coding tool (Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot). Human in the loop on every action. The agent is a tool. The engineer owns the outcome.

Level 2: autonomous system in production. Makes decisions, talks to APIs, handles real customers without human review on every call. The agent IS the product.

99% of agentic AI projects today are Level 1 dressed up as Level 2. The 40% Gartner is forecasting is the moment that gap becomes visible on the P&L.

A Level 2 agent is a 13-layer system:

1. Model/inference
2. Orchestration
3. Memory/context
4. Tools via MCP
5. Observability
6. Evals
7. Guardrails
8. Human-in-the-loop
9. Async runtime
10. Auth/multi-tenancy
11. Prompt version management
12. Cost/quota controls
13. Frontend/UX

Skip any of layers 5 through 12 and the agent either breaks silently, leaks data, or burns money you can't trace. 

The model is 5% of the build. 
The other 95% is where the 40% goes to die.

I've audited 14 agent projects this year where the team couldn't tell me which model version was running last week, who approved the last prompt change, or how much one customer query cost to serve. 

That's not a model problem. 
That's exactly the missing infrastructure that ends projects.

If you're scoping an agent project in 2026, ask your vendor to name 5 of the 13 layers. 

The answer will tell you whether you're in the 60% that ships or the 40% Gartner is forecasting.

Use the uploaded storyboard image as the main reference.
Create a 10-second cinematic Japanese TV commercial for the fictional energy drink “NOPE”.

Style:
Japanese high-end beverage commercial, cinematic realism, anime-inspired atmosphere, Makoto Shinkai × cyberpunk aesthetic, dark urban mood, wet neon reflections, film grain, premium commercial cinematography, dynamic camera motion, black + neon pink color palette.

Aspect Ratio: 16:9
Duration: 10 seconds
FPS: 24fps

Maintain consistency:
- same female character
- same NOPE can design and logo
- same rainy Tokyo cyberpunk atmosphere
- same neon pink lighting
- same cinematic continuity
Avoid face distortion, product deformation, extra objects, blurry logo, broken continuity.

Camera style:
smooth dolly-ins, macro close-ups, high-speed carbonation shots, subtle handheld motion during climax, premium commercial pacing.

Editing rhythm:
Start atmospheric → gradually intensify → explosive climax → clean hero ending.

----------------------------------------

----------------------------------------

Rainy Tokyo crossing at night.
Crowds move in slow motion.
A tired young Japanese woman walks through neon reflections on wet asphalt.
Low-angle slow dolly-in.
Lonely, emotionally numb atmosphere.

Narration:
「その毎日、まだ眠ったままか。」

Text overlay:
「刺激、足りてる？」

content:
生成AI時代、コードは何度でも書き直せる。アーキテクチャごと捨てて作り直せる。でもDBは違う。一度本番データが流れ込んだテーブル設計は、簡単には書き直せない。フレームワークの乗り換えとは桁が違う移行コストがかかる。何年技術が進歩しても、この重さだけは1ミリも変わらなかった。

本番運用が始まったDBは、もう自由に書き直せない。テーブルには外部キーが何重にも張られ、アプリは前提でクエリを書き、分析チームは毎日集計を流している。スキーマを変える瞬間、すべてが連動して動く。だから「あとで直そう」と先送りした設計判断は、半年後に数百万円の移行プロジェクトとして請求書が回ってくる。

技術選定で一番慎重になるべきDBが、現場では一番「とりあえず」で済まされる。自分も何度かやらかした。プロダクトの寿命を決めるのは流行のフレームワークではなく、最初のテーブル設計のほうだ。この観点から4冊を紹介します。

AIに作業させるだけじゃなく、
AIが作業中に何を考え、どこで迷い、何を変えたのかまで記録させる。

つまり、コードだけじゃなく
「意思決定ログ」まで残す。

これをやると何が起きるかというと、

・あとから修正しやすい
・なぜその実装になったか追える
・次のAIに引き継ぎやすい
・仕様と実装のズレに気づける
・人間がレビューしやすくなる

要するに、AIにコードを書かせる時代から、
AIに“実装の記憶”まで残させる時代に入ってる。

Claude Code / Codex / Cursorを使ってる人は、
この一文を入れるだけでマジで作業品質変わる。

「実装して」だけじゃなく、
「なぜそうしたかも残して」までがAIコーディング。

content:
【速報】
Claude Consoleに、「プロンプトキャッシュが効かなかった原因を特定できる機能」が追加されました😳
これ、簡単に言うと👇
Claudeに毎回同じ長い指示文を送るとき、
前に読んだ内容を再利用してAPI代を安くする仕組みがあります。
これが「プロンプトキャッシュ」です。

ただ、これまではキャッシュが効かなかった時に、
「どこが変わったせいでダメだったのか」
がかなり分かりづらかった。

今回の新機能では、Claude Console上で👇
・プロンプトのどの部分が変更されたのか
・なぜキャッシュにヒットしなかったのか
・その変更で何トークン分のコストが増えたのか
を確認できるようになりました。

つまり、今までは
「なんかキャッシュ効いてないな」
で終わっていたものが、

これからは
「この部分が変わったから、ここで余計にコストが発生してる」
まで見えるようになります。
AIエージェントや自動化をClaude APIで動かしている人ほど、
この差はかなり大きいです。
なぜなら、AI運用で怖いのは
気づかないうちにAPI代が積み上がることだから。

今回のアップデートで、
Claude APIのコスト管理はかなりやりやすくなりそうですね！
